cold: Every door is locked. Every window holds.
Nobody said anything about the floor.
d01: Day one. Liberty Mall, Thirty-fourth Street, Manhattan. Nine fifty-eight P.M.
You're the night janitor. Headphones in. So you don't hear the screaming.
When you look up, the street is full.
And the front doors are automatic. Every time one of them gets close, they slide open. Politely.
So you introduce the motion sensor to a fire extinguisher.
Then you drag over everything that isn't bolted down. The mall is closed.
d02: That means you have the one thing nobody else in this building ever had: the master key.
A hundred and forty stores. Eleven restaurants. A supermarket in the basement.
You check every gate, every door, every vent. Locked.
You are the only living person inside five floors of everything.
On the mall map, there's a little red dot. You write your name next to it. You are here.
d03: Day three. The phone network is dying. Calls fail. Your texts just sit there, sending.
You've written to Mom forty times.
Then, at four A.M., one bar. One message comes through.
It's from your little sister, Lily.
Mom says stay where you are. We're okay. Don't come home.
Then the bar is gone. You read it until the battery dies.
Then you charge it at the electronics store, and read it again.
d04: Day four. You learn the first rule from a mop bucket.
It hits the floor at seven A.M., and every head on the other side of the glass turns at once.
They can't see through the tinted windows. But they can hear.
So: soft shoes. No music. No slamming gates. You even oil the escalators.
For the next week, the loudest thing in Liberty Mall is you, breathing.
d05: Day five. Third floor. Something is scratching behind the gate of the pet store.
You open it with a broom over your head.
Inside: empty cages, a parrot that only says hello,
and one corgi puppy who has eaten an entire bag of treats, and is very, very happy to see you.
You name him Pretzel. He breaks the no-noise rule in about four seconds.
d06: Day six. The supermarket is in the basement, next to the old passage to the subway.
The passage is closed with a steel gate. Behind it, it's dark, and every now and then, something drips.
Then you fill four shopping carts with food and haul them upstairs.
You don't like the basement. And you get the feeling the basement doesn't like you either.
d07: Day seven. A week alive deserves a party.
Breakfast: a cinnamon roll the size of your head.
Lunch: every flavor of chips in aisle four, in alphabetical order.
Dinner: steaks on a grill from the sporting goods store, up on the roof, where the smoke can't trap you.
Pretzel gets a steak too. Dessert is a tub of ice cream and a ladle.
Tonight, you're the richest man in New York.
d08: Day eight. Fourth floor. Galaxy Arcade.
Two hundred machines, sound off, and you have the key to every coin box.
By sunset, every high score in the building is yours.
Then, the bowling alley. You've never been good at bowling. But you've got twenty lanes, and nobody watching.
Throw number four hundred and twelve: a perfect strike.
Pretzel is the only witness. He is not impressed. You'll need that arm later.
d09: You empty the party store, and fill the foam pit with three thousand balloons.
At the top of the highest jump, you can see out the top window, all the way to the Empire State Building.
It's dark. All of it. Not one light, in a city of eight million.
You fall back into the balloons, and you stay there a long time.
d10: Day ten. Across Thirty-fourth Street, twenty floors up, a light blinks. On. Off. On.
You grab a marker and the biggest poster in the mall, and you write: HI.
Ten minutes later, a sign appears in the window. HI. I'M ROSA.
For the first time in ten days, you laugh out loud.
Down on the street, forty heads turn toward the sound. You stop laughing.
d11: Day eleven. It rains all day.
You finally play the voicemail from Mom. The one from day one.
Hey sweetheart, working late again? I made lasagna. Lily saved you the corner piece.
You play it again. And again.
You don't notice you're crying until Pretzel licks your face.
Then: bang. A face hits the glass, right next to yours.
The window shakes. The window holds. Your heart almost doesn't.
d12: Day twelve. Rosa has a radio. Every evening at six, she writes the news on cardboard.
The army is evacuating Manhattan by helicopter. From rooftops.
But only from rooftops where they can see people.
Liberty Mall has a roof. You have no way to tell anyone you're on it.
That night, you fall asleep on a three-thousand-dollar mattress, thinking about how to be seen from the sky.
d13: Day thirteen. Two P.M. The power dies.
The freezers go quiet. The escalators stop mid-step.
The backup generator is in the basement, right next to the subway gate.
You go down with a flashlight and a hockey stick.
One pull. Two. The generator roars, and the lights come back.
And behind the steel gate, in the dark, something takes a step. Toward the noise.
d14: Day fourteen. You go back down. The padlock is fine. The gate is fine.
But the floor on the other side is wet, and in the wet, there are footprints. Bare feet. Dozens of them.
Coming up from the tunnel, stopping at the gate, and going back.
So now you know: the street isn't the only way in.
You take every bike lock in the sporting goods store. Twenty-two of them. All on the gate.
d15: Day fifteen. Halfway. You've built a routine.
Seven: push-ups. Nine: cleaning, because you're still the janitor.
Noon: roller skates through the food court. Three: cards with Pretzel. He cheats.
Ten: a movie in cinema six, alone, with a bucket of popcorn the size of a trash can.
It's a strange life. But it's a life.
d16: Day sixteen. You need the elevator to haul paint to the roof. You press the button. Ding.
The doors open. Gus, the night guard, is inside.
You thought he went home on day one.
He's been waiting in there for sixteen days, and he's very excited to see you.
You run. You lure him into the mattress store, slip out the back, and slam the gate.
Gus is now the only guard in the building who's locked in.
d17: Day seventeen. You paint a message on the roof.
Forty cans of white paint, letters ten feet tall: alive. One person. One dog.
It takes all day. Your arms shake.
That night, it rains. By morning, your letters are a pale gray smear.
Twice a day, the helicopters fly over the Hudson. Too far. Too fast. They never look your way.
d18: Day eighteen. The taps cough, then stop. No pressure. No water.
But in the middle of the atrium, there's a fountain.
Four thousand gallons, and about three hundred dollars in coins.
You boil it on the roof, a pot at a time.
It tastes like pennies and other people's wishes.
You make one of your own. Then you drink it.
d19: Day nineteen. Today is Lily's birthday. She's nine.
You bake a cake in the food court with a camping stove and a lot of hope. It collapses in the middle.
You put nine candles in it anyway. You sing to her photo. Quietly.
When you look up, there's a new sign in Rosa's window: Happy birthday, Lily.
She's never met her. She remembered anyway.
d20: Day twenty. Rosa's sign tonight is bad news. Last flights in ten days.
Ten days. Painted letters don't work. Shouting would bring the whole street.
Then you remember the party store. Thirty tanks of helium.
If you can't make a sign big enough for them to see, maybe you can send it to them.
You sit up all night, writing the same note, over and over.
d21: Six hundred notes, each one rolled up and tied to a string: Alive. Liberty Mall roof. Thirty-fourth Street. Please.
One pops right next to his face, and for one terrible second, the whole street goes silent and looks up.
Then they lose interest. You go back to work. Very, very quietly.
d22: Day twenty-two. Sunrise. You cut the net.
Six hundred red balloons lift off the roof of Liberty Mall, and drift east,
over Thirty-fourth Street, over the dark towers, over a city that forgot what color looks like.
Across the street, Rosa is in her window, both arms in the air.
Somewhere out there, somebody has to catch one. They just have to.
d23: Day twenty-three. Rosa's window is dark at six.
At seven, a new sign, written fast: They're in the building. Going to the roof.
Then her flashlight, moving up the stairwell, floor by floor, window by window.
You wait by the glass all night. Her light never comes back on.
d24: Day twenty-four. The mall is quieter than ever.
You talk to Pretzel. You talk to Gus, through the mattress store gate. He's a good listener.
You stop counting cans. You start counting days. Six left.
That evening, the sky over New Jersey turns green, then black.
The radio in the electronics store finally says something. A storm. A big one. Tonight.
d25: Day twenty-five. The storm hits at midnight. The rain is sideways.
Thirty-fourth Street becomes a river, and the subway entrances become waterfalls.
Somewhere under your feet, a hundred miles of tunnels are filling up.
And everything down there, everything that stood still in the dark for weeks, starts to move.
Up. Toward the air. Toward the only gate between them and you.
d26: Day twenty-six. The basement is flooding.
Brown water rolls through the supermarket, past aisle four, carrying cereal boxes like little boats.
At the subway gate, the water is waist-high. And behind the bars: hands. Dozens. Then hundreds.
Twenty-two bike locks are holding. For now.
You move everything upstairs and seal the basement door. Then you stand there, and listen to the bars bend.
d27: Day twenty-seven. If they get in, you'll need a way up. So you prepare.
Fourth floor: you line up every bowling ball in the alley at the top of the escalator. Sixty of them.
Then the mannequins. Ten of them, dressed in the nicest clothes in the mall.
Each one holding a phone. Each phone set to play music, at full volume.
The old rule was no noise. The new rule: noise on purpose.
d28: Day twenty-eight. Three A.M. You're in the food court, warming milk for Pretzel, when the hatch in the floor moves.
The flood pushed them up the service shafts. They didn't need the doors. They came from below.
You run. Up the dead escalator, Pretzel under your arm, forty of them right behind you.
Fourth floor. Sixty bowling balls. Four hundred and twelve throws of practice.
d29: Sixty bowling balls thunder down the escalator, and the first rows go down like pins.
Then you press play. Ten phones, ten mannequins, ten songs, all across the fourth floor.
The horde turns toward the noise. You and Pretzel climb to the roof and lock the door.
At midnight, the phones die. And they remember you.
They're at the door. The hinges are bending. No helicopter. No more plans.
d30: Day thirty. Dawn. The door is coming off its hinges.
And then, a sound. Rotors. A helicopter rises over the edge of the roof.
A soldier leans out, holding a red balloon. Your note.
And behind him, waving like crazy: Rosa. She made it.
She told them about the boy in the mall with the dog. The balloon told them where.
You grab the ladder, Pretzel in your jacket, just as the door gives way.
epi: And somewhere in Queens, there's a corner piece of lasagna with your name on it.
